Muchas gracias, Senor Vicepresidente, Excellencies, distinguished delegates. My heart goes out to the people of Haiti, often trapped between gang violence and heavy-handed responses. Despite some success in containing their activity in parts of the capital, Port-au-Prince, gangs continue to adapt and expand, reemerging in new areas and constantly rearming. Recent attacks in Kenscoff and Cressier and the growing gang presence in the Sud-Est department point to a strategy of seizing new territory and key transport routes, threatening stability across and beyond Haiti and leaving destruction in its wake. The first operations by the Gang Suppression Force, mandated by the UN Security Council, marked a long-awaited step towards greater security. But the force remains far below the strength needed. This week's renewal of its mandate needs to be followed by full, accelerated deployment with firm human rights safeguards embedded. During the reporting period from 1 January to 11 September this year, my office documented at least 5,700 people killed or injured by gangs or during operations against them. Gangs have also kidnapped more than 230 people and raped over 1,000 women and girls, and the real figures are likely much higher. Law enforcement operations continue to raise serious concerns about the unnecessary and disproportionate use of force. Since the beginning of the year, more than half of all casualties occurred in the context of security operations, with hundreds of people struck by stray bullets and explosive drones. The number of summary executions carried out by specialized police units has fallen significantly, by almost half, compared with 2025. However, people allegedly associated with gangs continue to be summarily executed. In some areas, so-called self-defence groups killed or injured some 280 people so far this year.

Vice-President, incessant violence has diverted resources that were needed for the protection of fundamental rights. Pillaging, looting and destruction of property paralyse economic activity. The permanent dangers prevent populations from reaching hospitals, schools and key services. More than half of Haitians face acute food insecurity, 40 per cent do not have access to basic healthcare, almost 1.5 million people have been forcibly displaced and many others still live with their bags always ready. Last year, 40 to 50 per cent of gang members were children. Recruitment and utilisation of children by the gangs almost tripled. For many children in Haiti, joining a gang can be the only means of survival, but no child should be forced to choose between his own life and the security of his neighbors. Children are exploited, victims of trafficking and ill treated, while the mechanisms that are meant to prevent those practices and to reintegrate children into society remain insufficient. Prisons are overcrowded to the maximum, with inhumane and degrading conditions throughout the country. Prisons are operating at triple their usual capacity. At least 25 people have died in detention this year alone. Free Equal elections are the only legitimate means of restoring constitutional order. However, in view of all that I have just described, it is hard to imagine that the necessary conditions for the holding of credible elections this year could be met. Those responsible for human rights abuses and grave violations should not be authorised to run at the elections.

This chaos has deep, intertwined roots, fed by greed and impunity, both within Haiti and beyond. The only way to cut those roots is through a comprehensive approach that looks beyond security. First, on sanctions. A handful of powerful individuals are exploiting and perpetuating people's grievances and the weakness of state institutions to pursue their own interests. These forces are strategic and well-resourced. Many gang leaders are subject to international sanctions. Those sanctions also need to cover all those pulling the strings behind criminal networks and benefiting from them. And they need to be matched by accountability on the ground to strengthen their practical impact. Second, on the arms embargo. To save lives and restore order, the continuous illicit flow of weapons and ammunition into Haiti must end. It is essential that the arms embargo imposed by the Security Council be fully respected and effectively implemented. States need to act urgently and decisively to crack down on arms trafficking and choke off these flows at their source. Third, on the diaspora. Nearly 5 billion US dollars in remittances flowed into Haiti last year, around one sixth of its GDP. These transfers are a lifeline for the country's economy and its people. Yet we are seeing a crackdown on Haitians who have fled abroad. In 2026, more than 220,000 people including nearly 20,000 children, have been forcibly returned to Haiti from several countries in the region. Many of these people fled for their lives or those of their families. Sending them back puts those lives at risk once again, in violation of the principle of non-refoulement. Fourth, on protection. I urge all States to support the rapid, full deployment of the Gang Suppression Force with the equipment it needs and in full compliance with human rights. The government needs to ensure that all security operations by state or private actors are firmly grounded in international human rights law. My office has provided human rights training to members of specialized police units and the Gang Suppression Force, and we are ready to do more. The authorities also need to prioritize strengthening the rule of law and the justice system to end impunity and to decongest prisons. Ensuring humane conditions of detention is paramount, particularly as the Gang Suppression Force scales up its operations. Fifth, on accountability. Two specialized judicial units supported by my office and the UN Office on Drugs and Crime are intended to help investigate mass atrocities, sexual violence and complex financial crimes. I urge the authorities to make them fully operational and all states to extend their support. There is also a need for broader efforts to fight corruption, poverty and inequality. This is key to lasting stability and essential to prevent gangs from preying on children. There is much work to be done and across all these areas, the Haitian government needs real, sustained and international support. Mr. Vice President, those who profit from the current state of disorder are determined to see Haiti fail. They seek to fray its social fabric and destroy the prospects of a stronger state. We cannot allow that to happen. We need all eyes on Haiti, and we must never lose sight of the fact that across the country, communities, Individuals are showing extraordinary courage, resilience, and dignity every day. Every morning, children leave homes without running water, dressed in immaculate, carefully ironed uniforms, and set out for school. We must help bring closer the day when hope, not fear, walks with them on the road. Thank you very much.

Distinguished delegates, it is the faces and voices of Haiti's children that I will never forget. During my visits to Haiti, I met with three boys between the ages of 12 and 16 who had been recruited by gangs. Their stories were remarkably similar, stories that can be multiplied by the thousands. Access to key services such as education and health must be extended. Core, alongside broader efforts to expand social protection and economic opportunity, deserves serious consideration. President, the member states in this room, the United Nations system, but most of all, the Haitian government, Haiti's business community and civil society should come together around a common objective, giving Haiti's youth a chance. Thank you, Mr. President. We welcome the Special Rapporteur's report. The Cambodian government claims that its human rights record is beyond scrutiny because it cooperates with the Special Rapporteur and other mechanisms and has ratified core human rights treaties. It claims that these reflect guarantees of human rights in the country. The reality, however, could not be further from this narrative. Civic and political space remain closed. Human rights defenders, journalists, and political opponents continue to be targeted with vague and overbroad criminal charges related to plotting, incitement, and defamation of the monarchy, based on evidence often obtained through digital surveillance and intrusion into private communications, and with the aid of a politicized judiciary. The continued imprisonment of the five young leaders of Mother Nature Cambodia is emblematic of this reality. The UN Working Group on Arbitrary Detention found that their detention is arbitrary and called for their immediate release. Yet, they remain imprisoned alongside over 100 other political prisoners. If the cycle of elections that begin next year were to have any semblance of credibility, at minimum, the government must take immediate measures to open civic and political space. It must amend criminal code provisions and other repressive legislation used to restrict freedom of expression and media freedom. peaceful assembly and association and release all political prisoners, including the Mother Nature Five. Implementation of the Special Rapporteur's recommendations is the real measure of Cambodia's cooperation with the mandate.

I thank you.

Thank you. I give the floor to Lawyers Rights Watch Canada.

Lawyers Rights Watch Canada, the International Commission of Jurists, The International Bar Association's Human Rights Institute and Lawyers for Lawyers agree with the Special Rapporteur that respect for human rights is key to resolving multiple crises in Cambodia. For decades, special procedures have urged Cambodia to ensure independence of the judiciary and legal profession, adequate independent legal aid, and independent and impartial investigations of rights violations. Yet Cambodia continues its long-standing pattern of harassment, unfair trials, arbitrary detention of human rights defenders, and transnational repression of defenders and dissidents, as well as impunity for unlawful killings and forced disappearances and abduction and refoulement of defenders to other countries. We condemn the enforced disappearances of Defenders Nguyen Duc Tuan and Chun Hiep, who were reportedly abducted on 18 September 2026 while en route to Thailand, and forcibly taken to Vietnam, where they now face fabricated terrorism charges. We urge the Council to call on Cambodia to implement recommendations of special procedures and treaty bodies, release all arbitrarily detained Defenders, and halt impunity for extrajudicial killings, enforced disappearances, and forcible renditions to other countries. We also ask what actions the Special Rapporteur recommends to curtail Cambodia's involvement in transnational repression. Thank you.

Thank you very much.

I give the floor to Human Rights Watch.

Mr. Vice President, Human Rights Watch thanks the Special Rapporteur for his report, which describes the deteriorating situation for civil society and the political opposition amid an unrelenting crackdown on freedom of expression. Cambodian authorities regularly charge opposition members, activists, journalists, and social media users with incitement and treason based solely on their peaceful expression. The judiciary acts at the behest of the ruling Cambodian People's Party. We are alarmed by the government's recent amendments to the commune administration law, which appear aimed at cementing one-party rule on the local level. Combined with the government's ongoing judicial harassment of opposition party leaders, including Rongchan and Thaksaita, the space for the political opposition is rapidly closing. Two journalists were sentenced to 14 years in prison on treason charges for reporting on border clashes with Thailand in February, while other journalists have been convicted for reporting on water shortages and cyber scam compounds. Five environmental activists from Mother Nature Cambodia are still detained in separate prisons after being arrested more than 800 days ago on baseless treason charges. Human Rights Watch urges the authorities to immediately release those detained for exercising the rights to freedom of expression, opinion, and assembly, and to drop politically motivated treason and incitement cases. We ask the Special Rapporteur what steps need to be taken between now and the June 2027 commune elections in order to ensure that polls are democratic and pluralistic. Thank you.
Thank you very much. I give the floor to Civicus.

Mr. Vice President, we welcome the report of the Special Rapporteur based on his recent visit to Cambodia. We are encouraged that he met with human rights defenders, environmental activists, representatives of CSOs, journalists and opposition politicians, including those detained. We also welcome the news that he is examining these cases and has raised concerns about their conditions. Of particular concern, he noted that over 100 people may be detained in Cambodia for exercising their civic freedoms. We remain concerned that repressive laws are routinely being misused by the Hun Manet government to criminalise and jail human rights defenders, such as the five Mother Nature environmental activists and those that oppose the CLV data agreement. Arrested individuals are frequently denied bail and held in prolonged pretrial detention. Peaceful protests are systematically suppressed, and there are excessive restrictions on CSOs under the Law on Association and Non-Governmental Organizations. Opposition politicians are also being targeted, and there are concerns that the repression is going to escalate ahead of local council elections scheduled for 2027. We call on this Council, all Member States and the UN Special Rapporteur to continue to engage with activists and civil society, push the government to drop all charges against activists and to release them immediately, as well as to repeal all restrictive laws and cooperate with the special procedures. We thank you.
Thank you. I now give the floor for a joint statement of the Inter-Spy Association.

The International Bar Association's Human Rights Institute, Lawyers for Lawyers, Article 19, Lawyers Rights Watch Canada, and Fora Major welcome the Special Rapporteur's recent visit to Cambodia and his report. We are concerned at the ongoing criminal prosecution of journalists in Cambodia for legitimate reporting. The recent decision of the Cambodian Supreme Court to uphold the 14-year prison sentences imposed on journalists **** Saphy and Peep Phera exemplifies this pattern. Such sentences are manifestly disproportionate and have a severe chilling effect on media freedom. This intimidatory use of the law against journalists is exacerbated by physical threats, restrictions and censorship of the media. These measures violate journalists' right to freedom of expression, and such restrictions do not meet international human rights standards. This has a wider impact on human rights in Cambodia. Without a free, independent media, other human rights violations go unreported and unaddressed. We are further concerned that this is compounded by the wider erosion of the rule of law, including the lack of an independent judiciary, attacks on lawyers, limits on civil society, and the silencing of political opposition. We call on Cambodia to immediately and unconditionally release all journalists that are arbitrarily detained, and call on this Council to keep monitoring the erosion of the rule of law in Cambodia, including attacks on journalists and lawyers.
Thank you. I now give the floor to the Xianxi Patriotic Volunteers.

我是国际爱国公约组织创始人，倡.

导爱国不能损害他国利益。我们认真阅读了特别报告员的报告，报告肯定柬埔寨在减刑打击网络欺诈方面的进展，也指出超百人因行使言论自由被拘。关于协会和非政府组织法律限制公民空间，边境冲突致数十万人流离失所。

国际爱国公约组织认为，应对这些挑战。

To respond to the challenges, the international.

Community should provide support rather than replace Cambodia's own efforts and must not serve as a disguise for external intervention. First, assistance should help Cambodia implement its existing commitments. Second, resources should be directed towards resettlement of displaced persons, screening of victims of telecom fraud. Third, all aid must answer one question, does it enhance Cambodia's capacity to resolve its own problems? The value of the report is not to put a label on Cambodia, but to help the international community deliver and effectively provide assistance. The International Patriotic to support all these efforts. Thank you.
I thank you and give the floor to Imam Ali's Popular Students Relief Society.

The UN Secretary-General and Special Rapporteur reports reveal a devastating reality: Cambodia's democracy is in freefall. As the upcoming elections approach, the ruling regime is trying to crush all genuine political pluralism and independent competition. We strongly condemn the censorship surrounding the border conflict. The Ministry of Information maintains an oppressive blockade, forcing the press to rely solely on state sources. At least 15 independent journalists have been summoned, arrested, or detained for reporting on the disputed Thai border. Furthermore, we condemn the regime's defrocking and immediate jailing of environmental monks on overbroad charges of incitement. Combined with the repressive Lango laws, these broader restrictions completely stifle free speech. True democratic elections are impossible under this severe blockade of information. Mesher, Special Rapporteur, given that Cambodia is systematically abusing national security laws to completely eliminate independent monitoring along the border, what concrete international enforcement mechanisms do you recommend to protect civilian journalists from being jailed for up to 14 years just for documenting this humanitarian conflict? Thank you.

I thank you.

This was the last speaker we could accommodate in this debate. I give the floor now to the distinguished representative of Cambodia, who is asked to divide his time available in two sections. He has one minute.

We thank all for the constructive engagement and support. and encourage fair assessment. Allow me to clarify on Thailand's false and misleading information as follows. The current displaced Cambodians were forced to flee from their home in Cambodian territory due to the Thai armed force attack in 2025. UN records confirm that Cambodian refugees from the 1970s civil war had already left Thailand in 1999. Cambodia and Thailand have a recognized international boundary under the 1904 convention and the 1907 treaty. The current Thai armed force activity in the illegally occupied area of Cambodia violate the UN Charter, international law and bilateral agreement. We categorically reject any misuse of online scam as a pretext for encroachment on another state territory. Commitment to combat online scam is clearly stated in my statement. I thank you.
Thank you very much. Distinguished, for the distinguished representative, I give the floor now to Mr. Andrews for his concluding remarks. You have six minutes.

Thank you again, Mr. Vice President and members of this Human Rights Council. I very much appreciate the attention, the comments, the questions, and the attention that you are placing on Cambodia and the particular challenges being faced by the people of Cambodia, and the human rights challenges that are being faced in that country. I'd like to group together some of the comments and questions, given the limited amount of time that I have to respond. But I want to say at the outset that my door is open. I very much welcome your continued engagement, your opinions, your recommendations. and your questions with respect to Cambodia and the role that I can play to help advance human rights, both in concept and in reality in Cambodia. So my door is open and I want to emphasize that to each and every one of you. First of all, let me address the border issue between Cambodia and Thailand, as you can appreciate, This is a very difficult and volatile issue. Emotions run high on both sides of this question. I have attempted to be as informed and as rooted in the facts and the truth as I possibly can. And I've done that by going to the border, by talking to people who have been displaced, by reaching out to Thailand and Cambodia to seek their views and perspectives on this crisis. And I want to say that my perspective, my comments, the things that I will be doing with respect to this conflict is based upon the human rights aspects of this conflict. I know that there are many, many issues surrounding the conflict, who started it, who initiated hostilities, for example. But these are issues beyond the scope of my mandate. My mandate is human rights and the human rights impacts of this conflict. And those are the that will continue to be the focus of my of my of my work. I am committed to providing you with whatever I can in terms of information. I am committed to the facts based upon my research and my findings. I am committed to engagement with both sides. And I am committed, as I said in my opening remarks, to supporting in any way that I possibly can the swift and peaceful resolution of this conflict, because the stakes could not be higher for those who are on that border. Economic opportunity has basically broken down. There is lots of suffering that is resulting on both sides of the border because of that lack of economic opportunity and engagement. There is so much at stake toward the resolution of this conflict, and I will do whatever I can through the prism of human rights toward that end. I'd like to just briefly mention the cyber scam issue that has been discussed and presented. In my report, of course, I talked about cyber scams, the importance of international engagement, and how the impact of that engagement can be seen with respect to cyber scams. But there are two issues that I included in my comments to the Government of Cambodia that I'd like to mention here. I stressed the need to hold accountable all of those who are responsible for those cyber scam operations, including those who are very, have upper levels of status in both the government and in business communities. Everybody should be held accountable. And secondly, I raised concerns about the status of those who have been victimized by virtue of being humanly trafficked into these cyber scam operations and suffering as a result. we need to do a much better job in identifying those who are victims and secure and support those victims. I'd like to point out in my report a range of things that I think actions that can be taken by the international community with respect to what can be done to advance human rights in Cambodia. I can't emphasize enough the importance of emphasizing and encouraging the release of all those who are in prison for exercising their fundamental human rights. We should be consistent and clear about the demand that every one of those people be released and that restrictions on the political activities and rights of those who were engaged in debates about the future of Cambodia particularly those who are preparing to engage in upcoming elections, commune elections next year, national elections the following year, that they have the right to do so. And the reason that's important is because the people of Cambodia deserve the right to choose their own future. And they should choose it on the basis of the information that they are provided freely and openly by candidates, political parties, and other advocates on all sides of the issues facing Cambodia. Let me just say in closing, Mr. Vice President and members of this Council, the Human Rights Council has been called the conscience of the United Nations. This is one of three pillars of this institution. And your responsibility holding that pillar is to advance human rights and to make the human rights of these issues shine clearly and brightly for all to see. I am honored to have this important responsibility as Special Rapporteur on the situation on human rights in Cambodia, and I commit myself to serving you and working with you toward that end. Thank you so very much.

Thank you very much.

That brings us to the end of this interactive dialogue. I wish to thank Mr. Andrews for his participation. We will take a short break before holding the interactive dialogue on the situation of human rights in Ukraine. Excellencies, distinguished colleagues, we'll now hold the interactive dialogue on the oral update of the High Commissioner on the situation of human rights in Ukraine, mandated by Council resolution 59/22. The list of speakers will close in 15 minutes. And I give the floor to Mr. Volker Turk, High Commissioner for Human Rights, to provide an oral update. Go ahead.

Muchas gracias, Senor Vice-President, Excellencies, distinguished delegates. The war in Ukraine is a human rights catastrophe that is growing and intensifying by the week, causing unfathomable pain to civilians and threatening an even greater disaster across the entire region. We need urgent action to end it in line with the United Nations Charter and international law. Against a backdrop of unceasing brutality, our recent report found shocking levels of sexual violence against civilians and prisoners of war. The Russian Federation is using these abhorrent acts to torture, intimidate, and coerce individuals and communities. Of more than 1,000 cases documented by my office, 89% were attributed to the Russian authorities and 11% to Ukraine. Most of the victims of sexual violence were men, particularly in places of detention, but women and children were also affected, primarily in occupied territory of Ukraine. This is just one terrible manifestation of the cruelty that has come to define this war. Alongside peace, there must be accountability. The full-scale invasion unleashed by the Russian Federation is killing and injuring hundreds of people every week, as front lines barely move. apartment buildings, schools, medical centers, railways, seaports, gas stations, shops, and logistics and telecommunication companies have been hit in recent attacks. The Russian Federation, as the aggressor, is inflicting immense suffering on Ukrainians. The Russian leadership should also consider what this war is doing to their own society, which is sinking deeper into fear, denial, and a militarized economy that puts death and destruction ahead of health care and education. I am shocked by the lack of empathy at display. Continuous escalation is creating a vortex of vengeance and reprisals that will have terrible consequences for people and communities for decades to come. Mr. Vice President, across Ukraine, people are living in constant dread. Air raid alerts in Kyiv were active for 33 hours during one 48-hour period earlier this week as missiles and drones rained down on the city. During the first eight months of this year, we verified some 15,280 civilians killed and injured on average, more than 400 every week for 34 weeks. This is 50% more than during the same period in 2025. On 19 September, for example, Russian long-range drone attacks killed four civilians, including three children, in the Kyiv region. On 12 and 13 September, one civilian was killed and 63 injured in attacks involving missiles and drones in the Odessa region. The number of civilian casualties in the Russian Federation has reportedly also increased. During the night of 19 to 20 September, the Russian authorities reported that three people were killed and 41 injured in a major missile and drone attack in the Moscow region. My office is unable to verify these reports fully. The authorities have not granted us access. Short-range drones kill and injure civilians, prevent the delivery of humanitarian aid, and restrict freedom of movement. Long-range drones are constantly expanding their reach and the threat they pose to civilians. Ukraine is a laboratory for drone warfare, and we need urgent steps at the international level to deal with the carnage wrought by these weapon systems around the world. But the situation near the front lines is of particular concern. Civilian casualties are at very high levels, caused by drone attacks, aerial bombardment, shelling, and systems that launch multiple rockets, devastating an entire area. In the Donetsk, Kharkiv, Sumy, and Zaporizhzhia regions, the use of aerial glide bombs by the Russian Federation has driven a significant increase in civilian deaths and injuries. In the first eight months of this year, these weapons killed and injured nearly 2,500 civilians, 62 percent more than during the same period last year. An estimated 2,000 people are trapped in Oleshky in desperate conditions without running water, electricity, or gas. Food deliveries have been severely disrupted, and the hospital is running out of fuel to run its generators. Mr. Vice President, attacks on energy infrastructure and commercial property have increased sharply in clear disregard of international humanitarian law. Russian attacks on supermarkets and food companies are already creating temporary shortages of vegetables and dairy products in some areas. Damage to power plants causes outages that affect water pumping stations and Russian forces have repeatedly attacked transportation infrastructure, including railways, ports, border crossings, and gas stations across Ukraine. As winter approaches, Ukrainians fear the worst is yet to come. Inside the Russian Federation, Ukrainian forces have reportedly struck warehouses and logistics centers belonging to major e-commerce companies, along with oil refineries. Russia's continued attempts to incorporate the Ukrainian territory it occupies, most recently by holding elections there earlier this month, are another blatant violation of international law. I'm alarmed by human rights violations linked to the presence of fighters from third countries in the war. My staff have interviewed prisoners of war from 36 countries who are held by Ukraine. Many said they were deceived into joining the Russian forces. Meanwhile, the massive use of explosives and mines is polluting ecosystems and creating new environmental risks. We do not yet know the full impact of toxic chemicals on land, rivers, and lakes. But it is clear that today's reckless warmongers oblivious to the harm they are causing future generations. Mr. Vice President, the conduct of this war to date cannot be allowed to dictate its future. We need a decisive shift towards de-escalation and peace. Rebuilding momentum towards negotiations is key. This calls for confidence-building measures based on human rights that could reduce the impact of hostilities on civilians. Such measures could include an agreement to end attacks on economic targets and energy infrastructure, local ceasefires on the front lines, enabling civilians to leave Oleshky, and a full exchange of prisoners of war respecting the principle of non-refoulement. These steps can be a basis for renewed efforts towards peace, grounded in human rights and in line with the UN Charter, international law, and General Assembly resolutions. We stand in solidarity with the civilians who are bearing the brunt of this war. To Russians, I say, this war is serving no one apart from a powerful elite, especially those with financial ties to the military. Its continuation will only lead to more shattered families and greater misery for ordinary people. To Ukrainians, I say, We are doing everything possible to support peace with justice and accountability. To the international community and particularly states with influence, I say, please take urgent action and to push for a negotiated peace now before this tragedy becomes even worse. Thank you.

Muchas gracias.

Thank you very much, the High Commissioner. According to our practice, we shall start the hearing from the delegations of the country concerned. The Russian Federation has indicated to the Secretariat that it will take the floor during this part of the list of speakers. I give the floor to the distinguished representative of Ukraine. You have five minutes.

Mr. President, Ukraine thanks the High Commissioner for his oral update and for presenting the thematic report on conflict-related sexual violence. which sheds light on deeply sensitive and important issues and provides credible, independently verified information on the situation. Its findings are devastating. During the reporting period, OHCHR verified 892 cases of conflict-related sexual violence perpetrated by Russian Federation authorities, including against 725 men, 151 women, 14 girls and two boys. Behind every figure is human being. Unfortunately, thousands of Ukrainian prisoners of war, political prisoners and unlawfully detained civilians remain in Russian captivity. OHCHR has documented the use of sexual violence as torture, intimidation, and coercion, while Russia has taken no visible steps to prevent, investigate, or prosecute such crimes. Russia must provide access to all Ukrainian prisoners and ensure their release. Mr. High Commissioner, Ukraine remains open to all UN monitoring mechanisms. We provide access to relevant institutions, information, and places of detention of prisoners of war. We are determined to uphold zero tolerance for violations under the 2627 UN-Ukraine implementation plan, together with UN mechanisms and the OEC. We are strengthening zero-tolerance policies on sexual violence and harassment across the security and defense sector, enhancing training and awareness, and advancing legislative changes. Every violation must be documented and investigated, regardless of the perpetrator's status. Mr. President, sexual violence is not the only one dimension of the suffering caused by Russia's war against Ukraine. Ukrainian civilians continue to be killed and injured every day. From 1st to 24th September alone, OCHA/CHR verified at least 200 civilians killed and 1,234 injured. Kyiv has come under repeated Russian attacks this month. On 25th September, Russian strike killed seven people, including 14 years old boy. 28th September attacks injured 24 people, including three children, and killed a woman. 30 September, another attack killed two people. On 1st October, Russian drones struck a Kyiv school where, uh, while more than 100 children and over 60 teachers were sheltering inside. Last night, Russia damaged the Southern Bridge, uh, in Kyiv and disrupted movement for hundreds of thousands of residents. This morning, a Russian strike hit a 25-story residential building in Kyiv and killed one person. These are combined by Russia's continued attacks on Ukraine's critical infrastructure, making the approaching winter an additional humanitarian challenge. This week, Kyiv already experienced disruption to electricity and water supplies. For Ukrainians, winter is not simply a season. It is another test of survival, test created by Russia. The situation is even more desperate in the territories under Russian occupation. In Oleshky, around 2,000 civilians, including nearly 50 children, remain trapped without adequate food, water, electricity, or medical care. We call on the international community, the UN, and humanitarian organizations to act urgently to secure humanitarian access and safe evacuation. Oleshky cannot be forgotten, and its civilians cannot be left at the mercy of the occupying Russian forces. Dear partners, we need your support. We need your support to protect civilians, strengthen air defense, support survivors and evacuation efforts, protect civilian infrastructure, and ensure accountability. There must be no normalization of civilian deaths, no impunity for sexual violence, no weaponization of hunger, darkness, or winter. Russia must stop its war against Ukraine, withdraw its forces, comply with international law, and be accountable for the suffering it has caused. Ukraine will remember every victim, and we will continue to work for justice. I thank you.

Thank you very much.

The list of speakers is now closed. I now invite interested delegations to ask questions or make comments on the oral update. Speaking time is one minute 30 seconds for all. I give the floor, on behalf of a group of countries, to the Minister for Foreign Affairs of Sweden, Maria Malmer Stenergard. That will be a video statement.

Mr. President, I have the honor to deliver this statement on behalf of the Nordic-Baltic countries. Every day, Russia chooses to continue its brutal war of aggression and deliberate attacks against civilians and civilian infrastructure in Ukraine. It shows that it is not interested in peace. The mounting reports of Russia's violations of international humanitarian law and international human rights law is appalling. Repeatedly, we learn about the horrific nature of Russia's violations. Torture of civilians and prisoners of war. Systematic sexual violence against detainees. Forcible transfer and deportation of Ukrainian children. We will not stay silent about these crimes. The Nordic-Baltic countries reaffirm our unwavering solidarity with the Ukrainian people and our steadfast support for Ukraine's independence, sovereignty, and territorial integrity. We will continue to demand full accountability for the crimes committed in the context of Russia's war of aggression against Ukraine. And we urge all countries to join this call for justice.

Thank you.

Muchas gracias.

Thank you very much. I give the floor to the delegation of the European Union.

Thank you, Mr. Vice President. The EU thanks the High Commissioner for his update. Russia's war of aggression against Ukraine continues to cause devastating harm and mounting civilian casualties. The Commission of Inquiry has concluded that Russian authorities have committed crimes against humanity of torture and forced disappearances, murder and forcible transfer of population, and war crimes, including deliberate, intensified targeting of civilians. The latest OHCHR report documents a shocking pattern of conflict-related sexual and gender-based violence. The overwhelming majority of verified cases is attributed to Russian authorities, including cases involving children. And yet, Russia has failed to take any discernible steps to prevent, investigate, or prosecute sexual violence committed by its personnel, which it chooses to shelter in impunity. The EU reiterates its resolute condemnation of the atrocity committed in Ukraine in the context of Russia's war of aggression and Russia's continuing violations of international law, including international human rights law and international humanitarian law in Ukraine. We reaffirm the EU's commitment to ensuring full accountability and justice for all international crimes and human rights violations. We reiterate our support for the International Criminal Court. We demand that Russia cease its aggression, withdraw all forces and military equipment from the entire territory of Ukraine, and fully respects Ukraine's sovereignty, independence, and territorial integrity within its internationally recognized borders. High Commissioner, how does Russia respond to your calls for engagement? Thank you so much.
Thank you very much. I give the floor to the representative of the Council of Europe.

Thank you, Mr. Vice President. On 30 September, the Council of Europe Register of Damage caused by the Russian aggression completed the opening of all the claim categories for compensation for damage, loss or injury caused by the wrongful acts in or against Ukraine. Claims can be submitted in 21 categories for individuals, 11 categories for legal entities and 11 categories for the State of Ukraine. The Register has so far received over 195,000 claims, 65,000 of which have been recorded. Behind them are human lives and a country shattered by war, which awaits justice, redress and reparation. Without that, there can be no just and lasting peace. Among the categories are death and disappearance of family members, personal injury, torture, sexual violence, forced displacement, loss of housing, employment, private enterprise, damage to infrastructure, cultural heritage, and environment. The Council of Europe is resolved not to let force take precedence over international law. The swift ratification of the Convention on the International Claims Commission should be the next step to enable the adjudication of claims. We count on progress on ratifications of the enlarged partial agreement on the Special Tribunal for the Crime of Aggression. These legal mechanisms are open to all countries who have voted for the respective resolution of the UN General Assembly. I thank you.
Thank you very much. I give the floor to the distinguished representative of Cyprus.

Thank you, Mr. Vice President. Cyprus thanks the High Commissioner for his update and for the continued work documenting the human rights consequences of Russia's war of aggression against Ukraine. We align ourselves with the EU statement. We welcome this report's focus on conflict-related sexual violence. We are concerned by widespread sexual violence against Ukrainian prisoners of war and civilian detainees. Even in their own homes, women and girls in occupied communities are at risk. The substantial number of male survivors also reminds us that sexual violence affects everyone. Sexual violence is prohibited under international humanitarian and human rights law and may constitute war crimes or crimes against humanity. Perpetrators must be held accountable. OHCHR identifies no discernible Russian steps to prevent, investigate, or prosecute these abuses. At the same time, we welcome Ukraine's cooperation with OHCHR, legal reforms, and steps towards urgent interim reparations. Survivors also need confidential, trauma-informed, age and gender-responsive assistance with a meaningful voice in shaping services. High Commissioner, how can OHCHR help ensure assistance reaches survivors, particularly those in occupied territory, facing barriers to reporting and care?

I thank you.

Thank you very much, Excellencies, distinguished participants. That brings us to the end of the meeting. We will reconvene this afternoon at 3 pm to continue the interactive dialogue on the situation of human rights in Ukraine, to be followed by the enhanced interactive dialogue on the High Commissioner's report on the Democratic Republic of the Congo. I hereby close the 37th meeting of the 63rd session of the Human Rights Council.
